section.title: The Sins of Eli's Sons
section.sectionRationale: Against the rising figure of the boy Samuel, the narrator sets the rotting priesthood of Eli's house. Hophni and Phinehas despise the LORD's offering and defile His sanctuary; Eli rebukes them feebly but honors his sons above God. A man of God then pronounces judgment: this priestly house will be cut off, both sons will die in one day, and God will raise up a faithful priest who serves before His anointed forever. It is one movement: the proud house falls while God prepares a faithful one.
section.thesis: The LORD who exalts the lowly also brings down the proud: Eli's sons treat His holy offering with contempt and honor themselves above Him, so their house is doomed, while in their place God promises to raise up a faithful priest who does His will and walks before His anointed, a promise that reaches beyond Samuel and Zadok to Christ.
section.frameNote: Four beats: the greed and contempt of Eli's sons, verses 12 to 17; Samuel growing between two households, verses 18 to 21; Eli's weak rebuke and his sons' hardness, verses 22 to 26; and the man of God's oracle of judgment and a faithful priest, verses 27 to 36.

units.label: The greed and contempt of Eli's sons
units.note: treating the LORD's offering with contempt

verses.text: Now the sons of Eli were wicked men; they had no regard for the LORD
or for the custom of the priests with the people. When any man offered a sacrifice, the servant of the priest would come with a three-pronged meat fork while the meat was boiling

and plunge it into the pan or kettle or cauldron or cooking pot. And the priest would claim for himself whatever the meat fork brought up. This is how they treated all the Israelites who came to Shiloh.

Even before the fat was burned, the servant of the priest would come and say to the man who was sacrificing, “Give the priest some meat to roast, because he will not accept boiled meat from you, but only raw.”

And if any man said to him, “The fat must be burned first; then you may take whatever you want,” the servant would reply, “No, you must give it to me right now. If you refuse, I will take it by force!”
Thus the sin of these young men was severe in the sight of the LORD, for they were treating the LORD’s offering with contempt.

units.label: Samuel growing between two households
units.note: the boy Samuel grew up in the presence of the LORD

verses.text: Now Samuel was ministering before the LORD, a boy wearing a linen ephod.
Each year his mother would make him a little robe and bring it to him when she went with her husband to offer the annual sacrifice.
And Eli would bless Elkanah and his wife, saying, “May the LORD give you children by this woman in place of the one she dedicated to the LORD.” Then they would go home.
So the LORD attended to Hannah, and she conceived and gave birth to three sons and two daughters. Meanwhile, the boy Samuel grew up in the presence of the LORD.

units.label: Eli's weak rebuke and his sons' hardness
units.note: they would not listen to their father

verses.text: Now Eli was very old, and he heard about everything his sons were doing to all Israel and how they were sleeping with the women who served at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting.
“Why are you doing these things?” Eli said to his sons. “I hear about your wicked deeds from all these people.
No, my sons; it is not a good report I hear circulating among the LORD’s people.

If a man sins against another man, God can intercede for him; but if a man sins against the LORD, who can intercede for him?” But they would not listen to their father, since the LORD intended to put them to death.
And the boy Samuel continued to grow in stature and in favor with the LORD and with man.

units.label: Judgment and the promise of a faithful priest
units.note: I will raise up for Myself a faithful priest

verses.text: Then a man of God came to Eli and told him, “This is what the LORD says: ‘Did I not clearly reveal Myself to your father’s house when they were in Egypt under Pharaoh’s house?

And out of all the tribes of Israel I selected your father to be My priest, to offer sacrifices on My altar, to burn incense, and to wear an ephod in My presence. I also gave to the house of your father all the food offerings of the Israelites.

Why then do you kick at My sacrifice and offering that I have prescribed for My dwelling place? You have {{kabad|honored}} your sons more than Me by fattening yourselves with the best of all the offerings of My people Israel.’

Therefore, the LORD, the God of Israel, declares: ‘I did indeed say that your house and the house of your father would walk before Me forever. But now the LORD declares: Far be it from Me! For I will honor those who honor Me, but those who despise Me will be disdained.
Behold, the days are coming when I will cut off your strength and the strength of your father’s house, so that no one in it will reach old age.
You will see distress in My dwelling place. Despite all that is good in Israel, no one in your house will ever again reach old age.
And every one of you that I do not cut off from My altar, I will cause your eyes to fail and your heart to grieve. All your descendants will die by the sword of men.
And this sign shall come to you concerning your two sons Hophni and Phinehas: They will both die on the same day.

Then I will raise up for Myself a {{neeman|faithful}} priest. He will do whatever is in My heart and mind. And I will build for him an enduring house, and he will walk before My {{mashiach|anointed one}} for all time.
And everyone left in your house will come and bow down to him for a piece of silver or a morsel of bread, pleading, “Please appoint me to some priestly office so that I can eat a piece of bread.”’”

kabad.gloss: To be heavy, to honor, to give weight to. The same root runs through the charge and the verdict: Eli honored his sons more than God, and God answers, those who honor Me I will honor, but those who despise Me will be disdained. To honor God is to give Him His true weight; Eli gave that weight to his sons instead.

neeman.gloss: Faithful, trustworthy, enduring, from the root aman, to be firm or reliable. God promises a neeman priest who does His heart and mind, and a neeman, enduring, house for him. In contrast to a faithless priesthood being cut off, God raises up faithfulness, a promise that reaches its fullness in Christ, the faithful High Priest.

mashiach.gloss: Anointed one, messiah. The faithful priest will walk before God's anointed forever. Already in chapter 2 the anointed King, first named in Hannah's song, reappears; priest and anointed King are bound together, a pairing fulfilled in Jesus, who is both the faithful Priest and the Anointed King.

basic.context: The narrator keeps switching between two pictures. On one side are Eli's sons, Hophni and Phinehas, priests who use their office to rob God and the people, seizing the best of the sacrifices by force and even defiling the sanctuary with immorality. On the other side is the boy Samuel, quietly growing up in God's presence, wearing his little robe. Eli scolds his sons weakly but will not restrain them, because he honors them above God. So a man of God arrives with a hard word: this priestly line will be cut off, both sons will die on one day, and God will raise up a faithful priest instead. The question is: what does God do with leaders who despise Him? He brings them down, and He raises up faithfulness in their place.
basic.hermeneutics: This is historical narrative with a strong moral and theological point, told by contrast: the corrupt house of Eli against the faithful child Samuel. It is not merely a warning to bad clergy; it shows God's holiness against those who treat holy things with contempt, and His faithfulness to raise up a true priest. We should feel the weight of the phrase they had no regard for the LORD, and the hope of the promised faithful priest, without turning the passage into a simple lesson on parenting.
basic.originalLanguages: The charge turns on the word kabad, to honor or give weight: Eli honored his sons more than God, and God replies, those who honor Me I will honor. In place of a faithless line God promises a neeman, a faithful and enduring, priest who does His heart and mind, and this priest will walk before God's mashiach, His anointed one. Priest and Anointed King stand together, and both meet in Christ.
basic.typology: The promised faithful priest who does all that is in God's heart points beyond the immediate fulfillments in Samuel and later Zadok to Jesus Christ, the truly faithful High Priest. The contrast between greedy shepherds who fatten themselves and the coming faithful one anticipates the Good Shepherd who lays down His life. And the pairing of faithful priest and anointed King foreshadows Christ, who is both.
basic.christ: God promises to raise up a faithful priest who will do whatever is in His heart and mind, with an enduring house, walking before His anointed forever. Samuel and later the priestly line of Zadok partly fulfill this, but the words strain beyond them. Only Jesus is the perfectly faithful Priest who always does the Father's will, whose house endures forever, and who serves as Priest before, and as, the Anointed King. Where Eli's sons treated the offering with contempt, Christ offered Himself as the one true sacrifice.
basic.god: God is holy, and He takes with deadly seriousness how His worship and His people are treated; contempt for His offering is a severe sin in His sight. He is just, cutting off a house that has despised Him even after generations of privilege. Yet He is faithful, refusing to leave His people without a true priest, and He binds His promise to His anointed one. He honors those who honor Him, and He will not be mocked.
basic.crossReferences: Hebrews 7 presents Christ as the permanent, faithful High Priest. Ezekiel 34 condemns shepherds who feed themselves rather than the flock. Malachi 2 rebukes priests who despise God's name. And 1 Peter 2 shows how God honors the One others rejected.
basic.oneStory: The same God who lifts the lowly Samuel brings down the proud house of Eli. The doom of a contemptuous priesthood and the promise of a faithful priest before God's anointed carry the story forward, past Samuel and Zadok, to Christ, the faithful High Priest and Anointed King in whom worship is finally made pure.

context.literary: The unit is built as an interleaved diptych: three brief notices of Samuel's growth, verses 18, 21, and 26, are stitched between two long blocks describing Eli's sons, verses 12 to 17 and 22 to 25, so that the reader's eye keeps swinging between a corrupt priesthood and a quietly maturing servant without either story pausing for long. This same alternating technique becomes the narrator's signature move; it will structure the rise of David against the decline of Saul across the rest of the book, so this passage is really the template the whole narrative learns to use. The man of God's oracle, verses 27 to 36, is itself carefully built: it opens by rehearsing history, God's ancient choice of Eli's father's house out of Egypt, moves through a direct accusation phrased as a question, why do you kick at My sacrifice, and only then pronounces sentence, first general, your house will be cut off, then devastatingly specific, both sons will die on the same day. That movement from remembered grace to indictment to sentence is a recognizable prophetic pattern that later oracles against Israel and the nations will repeat again and again. The chapter also plants a sign, the single day of two deaths, which the narrative will not let the reader forget; it is quietly resolved two chapters later, giving the whole unit a forward pull rare in ordinary narrative.
context.historical: The law specified exactly what priests could claim from a peace offering: the breast and right thigh after the fat had been burned to the LORD, Leviticus 7:28-34, a portion the worshiper handed over willingly once God's part was given. Eli's sons overturned that order at every point: they sent a servant with a three-pronged fork to plunge into the boiling pot and simply take whatever came up, and they demanded raw meat for roasting before the fat, God's portion, was even burned, which meant seizing the best cuts by threat of force and treating the LORD's own share as negotiable. To worshipers who had walked to Shiloh once a year with a costly animal, this was not petty theft but a public insult to the God they had come to honor. The women serving at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting, mentioned already at the tabernacle's founding in Exodus 38:8, held some recognized ministry role at the sanctuary; for the priests' own sons to seduce them there defiled the one place in Israel meant to be undefiled, compounding greed with sacrilege at the very door of God's presence. Unnamed prophetic figures called simply a man of God appear elsewhere in the historical books to deliver a single decisive oracle and then vanish from the story, a pattern this chapter shares; the emphasis falls entirely on the message, not the messenger. And a promised, enduring house was the highest honor a priestly or royal family could receive in the ancient world, which makes its revocation here all the more severe.
context.canonical: The sentence pronounced here is not left hanging; the narrative watches it come to pass with unusual precision. Both sons die on one day in chapter 4, exactly as the man of God foretold, and the wider doom on the house is completed generations later when Solomon strips the priesthood from Abiathar, Eli's descendant, and gives it to Zadok, 1 Kings 2:26-27, a move the narrator explicitly ties back to the LORD's word against the house of Eli spoken at Shiloh. From that point the priesthood in Israel runs through Zadok's line, later praised by name as the faithful priests in Ezekiel's vision of the restored temple, Ezekiel 44:15, standing in deliberate contrast to Levites who had gone astray, much as Eli's sons once had. There is a further irony worth noticing across the canon: an earlier Phinehas, Aaron's grandson, acted with zeal for the LORD's honor in Numbers 25:10-13 and received a covenant of an everlasting priesthood for it, while this later Phinehas, sharing his name, brings that same priestly line to ruin through the opposite spirit, contempt rather than zeal. The book of Malachi, centuries afterward, still measures Israel's priests against a covenant of life and peace given to a faithful priesthood, and rebukes those who corrupt it exactly as Eli's sons did, showing how long this failure kept troubling Israel's worship. The New Testament brings the whole thread to its resting point in Hebrews, where a priesthood that could be corrupted, exhausted, or cut off is replaced by one that cannot fail because the Priest Himself never dies, Hebrews 7:23-24.

hermeneutics.authorIntent: The writer is not simply recording an old scandal at a country shrine; he is warning every future reader who holds religious office that inherited privilege carries no immunity from God's scrutiny. Eli's house had been chosen out of all Israel, given the altar, the ephod, and a generous portion of every offering, precisely the kind of long-standing privilege that breeds a sense of entitlement, and the author wants readers to feel how far that privilege had been abused before judgment finally fell. He also intends the passage to teach patient discernment: the man of God speaks well before the sentence is carried out, showing that God warns before He acts and gives room, however brief, for repentance that in this case never comes. By setting the oracle's promise of a faithful priest alongside the sentence on Eli's house, the author means his audience to hold both truths together, that God's judgments on corrupt leadership are real and exact, and that His commitment to give His people faithful worship is never in doubt even when the leaders in front of them fail completely.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription: The passage narrates a specific verdict on one priestly family in one particular period of Israel's history; it does not establish a general rule that the sins of parents are automatically visited on every child, a principle Ezekiel later corrects directly by insisting each soul is accountable for its own sin, Ezekiel 18:20. Nor is Eli's failure meant as a fixed parenting formula, as though every mild mannered father will produce wicked sons or every strict one righteous ones; the text simply shows what did happen in this house, weak words without real restraint in the face of scandal that had become public knowledge. What does carry forward as abiding teaching is the principle beneath the history: leaders answer to God for how they use whatever authority He entrusts to them, correction offered without real consequence is not the same as faithful discipline, and honoring people above God, whoever they are, invites His judgment rather than His blessing.

debates.question: How can the sons' refusal to listen and God's intention to put them to death fit together, verse 25?

views.label: Judicial hardening after persistent sin
views.case: The sons had long treated God with contempt; the LORD's intention to put them to death is the judicial confirmation of a hardness they themselves chose, so their refusal to listen is both their guilt and God's righteous sentence unfolding.

views.label: God's sovereignty over even the wicked
views.case: The verse states plainly that the LORD intended their death, underscoring that God's purposes stand even over rebellious hearts, without excusing the sons, who remain fully responsible for despising Him.

debates.bearing: Either way the passage holds human responsibility and divine sovereignty together: the sons are guilty for their contempt, and God's just purpose is being accomplished; it warns against presuming on privilege while despising God.

debates.question: Who is the faithful priest promised in verse 35?

views.label: Fulfilled in stages through Samuel and Zadok
views.case: Samuel serves faithfully at once, and the enduring priestly house is realized in Zadok's line, confirmed under Solomon when Eli's descendant Abiathar is removed; the promise finds real historical fulfillment in Israel's priesthood.

views.label: Ultimately fulfilled in Christ
views.case: The language of a priest who always does God's heart, with a house enduring forever and serving before the anointed for all time, strains beyond any Old Testament priest and is answered only in Jesus, the faithful High Priest, Hebrews 7.

debates.bearing: Both are true in sequence: the promise unfolds through Samuel and Zadok yet reaches its fullness in Christ, so that the reader looks past every faithful but mortal priest to the everlasting one.

debates.question: Was Eli himself a genuinely godly man despite his failure with his sons?

views.label: A basically faithful man who failed as a father
views.case: Eli's own devotion, his years of quiet service, his prayer for Hannah, and his final submission that He is the LORD, let Him do what is good in His eyes, all suggest real personal piety compromised by parental indulgence rather than complicity in his sons' sin.

views.label: A leader whose passivity made him complicit
views.case: The man of God addresses Eli directly, why do you kick at My sacrifice, you have honored your sons more than Me, charging Eli himself with sin, not merely his sons, since knowing of wickedness and failing to restrain it functions as a kind of participation, 1 Samuel 3:13.

debates.bearing: The text holds Eli responsible for what he tolerated even while granting his personal faith was real, warning that indulgent inaction toward known sin is itself a moral failure, not neutral inaction.

study.originalLanguages: Beyond kabad, neeman, and mashiach, the passage is threaded with other telling words. The narrator brands Eli's sons at the outset beney beliyya'al, literally sons of worthlessness or sons of Belial, the same blunt idiom Judges uses for the men of Gibeah and Deuteronomy for those who lead a town astray; it is the Old Testament's harshest label for a scoundrel, marking Hophni and Phinehas as beyond ordinary rebuke from their very introduction. Verse 13 calls their extortion a departure from the mishpat, the custom, of the priests with the people, yet mishpat is the ordinary Hebrew word for justice or rightful due; the same men who insisted on their mishpat, their entitlement, abandoned mishpat, justice, toward the very worshipers they served, and the Hebrew lets that irony sit unexplained. The instrument itself, the mazleg, the three pronged meat fork plunged into the boiling pot, is a rare, concrete word for sanctuary equipment, grounding the scandal in an exact, almost forensic physical detail rather than a vague charge. The servant sent with that fork is called a na'ar, a boy or young attendant, precisely the same word the narrator uses again and again for Samuel himself; Hebrew quietly sets two boys side by side in this chapter, one na'ar exploiting the altar for his masters' greed, another na'ar growing to serve it in truth. When Hannah later conceives again, the text says the LORD paqad, attended to or visited her, the verb used of God's decisive visitations elsewhere in Scripture, most notably when He tells Moses that He has paqad, attended to, His people in their affliction, Exodus 3:16, linking Hannah's quiet blessing to the pattern of God's great historical acts of attention. Samuel's growth is marked by gadal, to grow great or grow up, repeated at verses 21 and 26, an unhurried, organic verb that stands in deliberate contrast to the sudden, violent cutting off promised for Eli's line. And the final notice that the boy grew in chen, favor, with the LORD and with man, uses the same word for the grace found by Noah, Genesis 6:8, and will resurface almost verbatim of another boy centuries later, whose favor with God and man Luke likewise records, Luke 2:52. Running beneath all of this is the single word bayit, house, repeated across the whole oracle, your father's house, your house, an enduring house for the faithful priest, so that the entire passage is, in the Hebrew, a contest between houses, whose weight will stand and whose will be cut off.

typology.type: The promised faithful priest who does all God's heart
typology.fulfillment: God promises to raise up a priest who does whatever is in His heart and mind, a description no merely human priest, however devout, could ever satisfy completely, since even Zadok's line eventually failed and was itself replaced. Hebrews applies exactly this kind of description to Jesus, the merciful and faithful High Priest who was tempted in every way yet never sinned, and who is able to sympathize with weakness because He shares our humanity while remaining perfectly obedient to the Father's will, Hebrews 2:17 and 4:15. Where Samuel and Zadok were faithful for a lifetime, Christ's faithfulness never lapses and never ends, since He continues forever, Hebrews 7:24.

typology.type: The greedy priests fattening themselves versus the faithful one to come
typology.fulfillment: Ezekiel later condemns shepherds of Israel who feed themselves, eating the choice meat and clothing themselves with the wool, while neglecting the sheep entirely, language that reads like a commentary on exactly what Hophni and Phinehas did with the LORD's own offerings. Jesus deliberately answers that indictment by naming Himself the Good Shepherd who lays down His own life for the sheep rather than seizing anything for Himself, John 10:11. The contrast is total: Eli's sons took meat meant for others and kept their own lives; Christ gives His own life so that others may be fed.

typology.type: The faithful priest walking before the anointed one forever
typology.fulfillment: The oracle pairs two future figures, a faithful priest and God's anointed one, walking together before the LORD, a pairing Israel's history keeps as two separate offices, king and priest, held by different men and often in tension, as when King Uzziah is struck with leprosy for intruding on priestly incense, 2 Chronicles 26:16-21. Hebrews declares that Jesus holds both offices at once without confusion or rivalry, a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek, who was himself both king and priest, Hebrews 7:1-3 and Psalm 110:4, so that the ancient pairing this oracle names is finally united, not merely accompanied, in one person.

typology.type: The house honored above God, and the house that endures
typology.fulfillment: Eli was warned that far be it from Me reverses an earlier promise that his father's house would walk before the LORD forever, showing that even a house once granted apparent permanence could be revoked for unfaithfulness. Christ's house, by contrast, is built not on inherited privilege but on His own perfect obedience, and it cannot be revoked because He never gives God occasion to say far be it from Me; He is the Son who was faithful over God's house as a son, not merely a servant within it, Hebrews 3:5-6, so that everyone built into that household inherits a security no priestly line before Him could offer.

study.christ: The reversal embedded in verse 30 deserves close attention: God had once said that Eli's father's house would walk before Him forever, yet that promise, given to a house that proved unfaithful, is explicitly overturned, far be it from Me. Every conditional privilege in Israel's history eventually meets this same limit, priesthood, land, even the temple itself, because each rests on human faithfulness that fails. The gospel answers this pattern by grounding the ultimate priesthood not in a family's ongoing obedience but in the finished obedience of one man who cannot fail retroactively, since His faithfulness is already complete; Christ's priesthood cannot be revoked the way Eli's was because nothing remains to go wrong. The sign given to Eli, that his sons would die on the same day, functioned to authenticate the whole oracle in advance, proving that God's harder word, the promise of a faithful priest still future, could also be trusted precisely because the near sign came true exactly as spoken. Jesus offers His own generation a comparable authenticating sign centuries later, refusing every request except the sign of Jonah, three days in the heart of the earth answered by three days in the tomb, Matthew 12:39-40, so that His resurrection functions exactly as Hophni and Phinehas's death once did, a fulfilled sign that guarantees every larger promise bound up with it. Where the sign in Samuel's day proved a word of judgment, the sign of Jonah proves a word of salvation, the decisive difference between the shadow and its substance. And the very words the man of God uses of the future priest, he will do whatever is in My heart and mind, describe exactly what Jesus says of Himself, that He always does what pleases the Father, John 8:29, and that He came not to do His own will but the will of Him who sent Him, John 6:38, so that the oracle's ancient hope reads, in hindsight, like a description written for Him alone.
study.god: What stands out about God's dealing with Eli's house is the sheer patience that precedes the sentence. The oracle reminds Eli that his father's house was chosen out of Egypt itself, centuries before this scene, and had enjoyed the altar, the ephod, and a generous share of Israel's offerings the whole time; God does not move quickly here, He has carried this family's privilege for generations before finally saying, far be it from Me. That patience should not be mistaken for indifference; when the sentence comes it is total, and the reader is meant to feel the weight of how long divine patience had already been extended before it ran out. The passage also raises, without resolving neatly, one of Scripture's harder claims about divine sovereignty: they would not listen to their father, since the LORD intended to put them to death. This does not erase the sons' own guilt, spelled out at length in their extortion and immorality, but it does show that God's righteous judgments can work themselves out even through a hardened refusal to hear correction, much as Pharaoh's own hardened heart both expressed his stubborn character and served God's larger purpose in the exodus story. God is never made the author of the sin itself, only the sovereign Lord who ensures that persistent, willful sin meets its appointed end on His timetable rather than escaping consequence. Notice, too, how personal God makes this word: He does not send a general decree about priestly corruption but addresses Eli by name, in the first person, why then do you kick at My sacrifice, you have honored your sons more than Me. This is not a distant deity auditing an institution from afar; it is the LORD speaking as one who has been personally slighted, whose own offering has been treated with contempt, and who cares enough about being honored rightly to confront the offender directly rather than merely tabulating the wrong from a distance.

crossReferences.note: The law fixed exactly what a priest could claim from a peace offering, the breast and right thigh, after the fat had been burned to the LORD. Hophni and Phinehas overturned this order at every point, seizing raw meat by force before the fat was even offered, turning a lawful, limited portion into unrestrained theft from God and from the worshiper alike.

An earlier Phinehas, Aaron's grandson, acted with zeal for God's honor and received a covenant of an everlasting priesthood for it. The later Phinehas of this chapter, sharing his name, brings that same priestly line toward ruin through the opposite spirit, contempt rather than zeal, a bitter irony the shared name only sharpens.

Centuries later Malachi rebukes priests who despise the LORD's name, offer blemished sacrifices, and cause many to stumble by their instruction, measuring an entire later generation of priests against the same charge leveled here against Eli's sons, showing how long this particular failure kept recurring in Israel's worship.

God tells Moses that He has attended to His people and seen what is done to them in Egypt. The same verb describes the LORD attending to Hannah later in this chapter, quietly placing her private blessing within the pattern of God's great, historic acts of remembering and acting for His people.

The sign given here, that Hophni and Phinehas would die on the same day, is fulfilled exactly two chapters later when the ark is captured and both sons die in the same battle, confirming that the LORD's harder, longer term promise of a faithful priest can also be trusted.

Solomon removes Abiathar, Eli's descendant, from the priesthood and gives it to Zadok, and the narrator explicitly says this fulfills the LORD's word against the house of Eli spoken at Shiloh, showing the oracle's reach extending across generations to its final, historical completion.

God condemns shepherds who feed themselves, eating the choice meat and wearing the wool, while the flock goes hungry and scattered, language that reads almost like a commentary on the very sin of Eli's sons, who fattened themselves on offerings meant for the LORD and the people.

Jesus names Himself the Good Shepherd who lays down His own life for the sheep, the deliberate reversal of shepherds who take life and comfort for themselves; where Hophni and Phinehas seized meat meant for others, Christ gives up everything, including His own life, for those He serves.

Moses was faithful in God's house as a servant, but Christ is faithful over God's house as a son, whose house we are if we hold firmly to our confidence, a permanence no priestly family under the old covenant, including Eli's, could ever offer its members.

Many priests were prevented by death from continuing in office, but Jesus holds His priesthood permanently because He continues forever, and is therefore able to save completely those who come to God through Him, always living to intercede, exactly the enduring house this oracle first promised.

study.oneStory: Every priesthood in Scripture exists to solve the problem opened in Eden, how sinful people can safely stand in the presence of a holy God, and this chapter shows how quickly even a divinely appointed solution can become another instance of the very problem it was meant to fix. Eli's sons were given unearned access to God's altar and His people's offerings, much as Adam was given unearned access to the garden and its abundance, and both turned privileged nearness to God into an occasion for self-serving grasping rather than grateful service. The oracle against Eli's house therefore functions like a small, local re-enactment of the fall, trust betrayed, privilege abused, judgment following, but it also carries the story forward rather than merely repeating it, because God does not simply remove a failed priesthood and leave a vacancy; He promises, even in the act of judgment, to raise up a faithful one. That promise threads through the rest of the Old Testament story, through Zadok's more stable line, through the ongoing priestly service in the temple, all of it straining toward something the text itself admits none of these arrangements fully satisfies, an enduring house, a priest who always does God's heart. The New Testament identifies that priest as Jesus, whose single, sufficient priesthood ends the entire long history of priests who could fail, die, or be removed, and who opens access to God not through inherited office but through His own finished obedience. And Scripture's last chapters describe God's redeemed people themselves made a kingdom of priests to our God, Revelation 5:10, so that what began as one family's exclusive, and finally forfeited, privilege becomes, in Christ, a status shared by everyone who belongs to Him, the failed priesthood of Eli's house answered at last by a priesthood that cannot fail and is no longer reserved to a few.

quiz.q: What made the sin of Eli's sons so severe in the LORD's sight?

options.text: As priests they treated the LORD's offering with contempt, robbing God and the people and defiling His worship.
options.note: Verse 17 names their contempt for the LORD's offering as the heart of the sin.

options.text: They took portions of the sacrifices by force before the fat was burned.
options.note: True and part of it, but the deeper charge is contempt for God and His worship, not only greed.

options.text: They failed to keep proper records of the sacrifices.
options.note: The issue was contempt and abuse, not administrative failure.

options.text: They offered too many sacrifices to the LORD.
options.note: The opposite; they abused and despised the offerings, not offered too many.

quiz.q: What does God's word to Eli, those who honor Me I will honor, reveal?

options.text: Eli gave the weight of honor to his sons that belonged to God, and God repays honor with honor and contempt with disdain.
options.note: The word kabad ties the charge and the verdict together, verses 29 to 30.

options.text: God rewards those who respect Him and judges those who despise Him.
options.note: True, but misses that the specific charge was honoring his sons above God.

options.text: God simply wanted Eli to speak more sternly to his sons.
options.note: The issue was misplaced honor, not merely a firmer tone.

options.text: God promised to honor Eli's house no matter what they did.
options.note: The opposite; the house is cut off for despising Him.

quiz.q: Who is the faithful priest God promises to raise up in verse 35?

options.text: One fulfilled partly in Samuel and Zadok but ultimately in Christ, the everlasting faithful High Priest.
options.note: The promise unfolds in history yet reaches its fullness in Jesus, Hebrews 7.

options.text: Samuel and later the priestly line of Zadok.
options.note: A true stage of fulfillment, but the language of a house enduring forever points beyond them to Christ.

options.text: Eli himself, restored after his repentance.
options.note: The promise stands against Eli's house, not for its restoration.

options.text: No one; it was an empty threat.
options.note: God really does raise up faithful priesthood, fulfilled finally in Christ.

quiz.q: How does the narrator use the boy Samuel in this passage?

options.text: He sets Samuel's quiet growth in God's favor against the corruption of Eli's sons, a rising figure against a falling house.
options.note: The alternating notices of Samuel, verses 18, 21, 26, contrast the two households.

options.text: He shows Samuel growing up faithfully at the sanctuary.
options.note: True, but the point is the deliberate contrast with the falling house of Eli.

options.text: He presents Samuel as one of Eli's wicked sons.
options.note: Samuel is the opposite of Eli's sons, not one of them.

options.text: He includes Samuel only by accident, with no purpose.
options.note: The contrast is deliberate and structural.

quiz.q: How does this passage point forward to Christ?

options.text: It promises a faithful priest who does all God's heart and serves before His anointed, fulfilled in Jesus the faithful High Priest and Anointed King.
options.note: The oracle joins faithful priest and anointed one, both met in Christ.

options.text: It contrasts greedy shepherds with a coming faithful one.
options.note: True, but leaves out that Christ is both the faithful Priest and the anointed King the promise names.

options.text: It teaches only that bad priests will be punished.
options.note: Judgment is real, but the forward-looking promise of a faithful priest is the point that leads to Christ.

options.text: It has no connection to Christ.
options.note: The promise of a faithful priest before the anointed clearly points to Jesus.

questions: Eli's sons treated holy things with contempt because they had no regard for the LORD. Are there ways you handle God's worship, word, or gifts casually, without giving Him His true weight?
Eli honored his sons more than God. Is there a relationship or loyalty in your life that you are quietly placing above your loyalty to the LORD?
Eli rebuked his sons but would not truly restrain them. Where might God be calling you to loving but firm action, rather than words that cost you nothing?
God promised a faithful priest even as a faithless one fell. How does it comfort you that Jesus is the faithful High Priest who always does the Father's will and never fails?
The passage says God honors those who honor Him. What would it look like this week to give God the weight and first place He deserves in your decisions?

translationNotes.note: God can intercede for him renders a term the BSB footnote allows as the judges; the sense is that a human mediator can address wrongs between people, but sin against the LORD Himself is graver.
The verbs honor and despise translate forms of kabad and its opposite; the same root ties Eli's fault, honoring his sons, to God's verdict, honoring those who honor Him.
The BSB follows the Dead Sea Scrolls and Septuagint reading that his descendants will die by the sword; the Masoretic Text reads will die as mortals, or in the prime of life.
